Combination with the partner's broader advertising datasets can strengthen such inferences.
assumptions: Assumes the partner has auxiliary datasets and the analytics are segmented enough to support behavioral or demographic inference.
uncertainty_note: Detailed subtree citation is approximate; the inference risk itself is strongly applicable.

title: Aggregated reports may disclose information about identifiable or very small groups
description: If the backend shares analytics for narrowly defined cohorts, rare events, low-volume regions, or niche feature combinations, the partner may learn information about identifiable individuals or very small groups despite the data being labeled aggregated. This is especially relevant where counts are low or where outliers dominate a cohort.
assumptions: Assumes no robust aggregation thresholds, suppression, noise addition, or k-anonymity-style controls are enforced before sharing.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; disclosure from insufficient aggregation is the main concern.

title: Sharing analytics with an advertising partner may create unawareness about secondary use
description: Users may be unaware that their app usage contributes to analytics shared with an external advertising/analytics partner to fund the free tier, particularly if notices are vague or bundled. They may not understand the recipient, the monetization purpose, retention, onward sharing, or profiling implications.
assumptions: Assumes transparency is incomplete, hard to find, or not presented at the time data is collected or shared.
uncertainty_note: Applies at the destination because the partner's receipt and subsequent use contribute to the user's lack of awareness; exact subtree id is best-judgement.

title: Analytics sharing for ad-funding may be incompatible with user expectations or consent basis
description: Sending usage and engagement analytics to an advertising/analytics partner for monetization may exceed what users reasonably expect from core app operation, especially if the free tier does not clearly separate necessary analytics from partner-sharing for advertising or funding purposes. This can create non-compliance with consent, purpose limitation, data minimization, or transparency obligations.
assumptions: Assumes the legal basis, consent mechanism, opt-out, and contractual controls for partner use are absent, weak, or not aligned with the actual sharing purpose.
uncertainty_note: Compliance conclusions depend on jurisdiction and actual notices/consent flows; threat is plausible but context-dependent.

title: Check-in/SOS message content identifies the child
description: The manual check-in/SOS payload contains the child's current location and is inherently tied to the child sender, allowing the backend to identify or single out the child from the message and associated account/session metadata.
assumptions: The child uses an authenticated app account, device identifier, or stable session so the backend can associate the message with a specific child.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include identity threat-tree details.

title: Real-time location disclosure to the backend
description: The child discloses precise current location together with an SOS/check-in event to the backend. This reveals highly sensitive contextual information about whereabouts and potentially emergency status.
assumptions: The backend receives precise or near-real-time geolocation rather than coarse location only.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include disclosure threat-tree details.

title: Repeated check-ins/SOS events enable linkability of the child's activity
description: Multiple manual check-ins or SOS messages sent over time can be linked by the backend using account, device, network, or message metadata, enabling correlation of separate events into a behavioral history for the same child.
assumptions: The backend stores persistent identifiers or metadata across messages.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include linkability threat-tree details.

title: Location check-ins allow inference of routines and sensitive places
description: Even if only explicit location is sent, the backend can derive additional personal information such as home/school locations, daily routines, social relationships, religious attendance, health visits, or distress patterns from repeated check-in/SOS submissions.
assumptions: The backend retains historical submissions or can analyze patterns across multiple events.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include detectability/content-unawareness threat-tree details.

title: SOS/check-in creates attributable evidence that the child sent a message from a location
description: The transmitted message can serve as attributable evidence that a specific child initiated a check-in or SOS at a particular time and place. This may later be used to deny the child plausible deniability about having sent it.
assumptions: The backend logs sender identity, timestamp, and location with sufficient integrity to attribute the event.

title: Child may be unaware of backend-side retention and secondary use of SOS/location data
description: A child may not understand that sending a manual check-in/SOS shares not only the immediate alert but also precise location, timestamps, and metadata with the backend, potentially for storage, analytics, or later review.
assumptions: The app UX does not fully explain backend processing, retention, and onward sharing in a child-comprehensible way.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include unawareness threat-tree details.

title: Collection of child's precise location during SOS/check-in may exceed necessity or valid consent basis
description: The backend's receipt and processing of a child's precise location and emergency-status message may violate data minimization, purpose limitation, child-specific transparency, or parental-consent/legal-basis requirements if broader data than necessary is collected or retained.
assumptions: Applicable law/policy requires necessity, proportionality, child-appropriate transparency, and possibly parental authorization for processing children's location data.
